claims.text: Local compositional fluctuations act as dynamic obstacles to dislocation motion during high-strain-rate deformation in high-entropy alloys.
These compositional obstacles enhance strength.
These compositional obstacles simultaneously enhance ductility.
Mixing several principal elements can produce an HEA that is uniform in overall composition while retaining local nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
Localized nanoscale compositional fluctuations create heterogeneous energy barriers to dislocation motion.
Dislocations interact with dynamic compositional clusters that temporarily block or slow their motion.
At high strain rates, compositional clusters provide additional strengthening.
Multidirectional deformation mechanisms allow the alloy to retain ductility despite obstacle strengthening.
Under dynamic loading, the HEA will have higher yield strength than the conventional-alloy baseline.
Under dynamic loading, the HEA will have greater ductility than the conventional-alloy baseline.
Dislocations will interact with compositional fluctuations more frequently in the HEA than in the baseline alloy.
A conventional alloy can be designed with an average elemental composition similar to that of the HEA but with minimal local compositional fluctuations.
The baseline alloy's minimal local compositional fluctuations result from limited entropy effects.
The proposed mechanism should apply when multiple principal elements induce significant local compositional variations.
The proposed mechanism should apply at strain rates high enough to activate dynamic dislocation-obstacle interactions.
The mechanism may cease to be dominant at temperatures near recrystallization.
The mechanism may cease to be dominant in alloys containing too few principal elements.
Deformation twinning or phase transformation may also contribute to the dynamic mechanical response.
Side-by-side dynamic tests with nanoscale compositional mapping and in-situ dislocation imaging can test the proposed correlation.
Failure to observe improved strength or ductility, or failure to observe more frequent fluctuation-dislocation interactions, would falsify the hypothesis.
